# Binary Search Tree, Drawn (C)

A **binary search tree** keeps every value smaller than a node in its left branch and every larger one in its right. To find a value, start at the top and go left or right at each node: with a good shape, each comparison rules out about half of what's left, so a million values take about 20 comparisons.

The catch is in "with a good shape". The tree's shape comes from the **order the values arrive in**. The question here: **how much does the insert order matter?** You can watch each insert walk down the tree, and then measure it.

How the cells run:

- **C runs in your browser.** xcc compiles the cell to WebAssembly on the page, so it runs at once, on the website too. It shares its trees by printing a `__NB_SET__` line.
- **The player is an HTML cell** that reacts at once to the dropdown, and **JavaScript** checks the trees and charts the cost.

*Binary Search Tree, Drawn* is the same notebook with real Java in the Debian VM, in the DevTools Hub. Both use the same generator and build the same trees, number for number.

> ✨ The code cells were written by an AI model from prompts, and each prompt is saved in its cell: press **✨** in a cell's header to see it.

Press **Run all**.

## 1. Pick an insert order

> Controls, 900 pixels wide: a dropdown "Insert order" bound to bst_order with Balanced (middle first), Random, Sorted and Alternating (smallest, largest, …), values balanced, random, sorted and alternating, default balanced.

The same 15 values, put in four different orders. A binary search tree keeps every value smaller than a node on its left and every larger one on its right, so **the order you insert in decides the shape**. The player below switches as soon as you pick.

ai.prompt: Controls, 900 pixels wide: a dropdown "Insert order" bound to bst_order with Balanced (middle first), Random, Sorted and Alternating (smallest, largest, …), values balanced, random, sorted and alternating, default balanced.

## 2. Build the trees in C

> In C, build binary search trees in plain arrays (value, left, right, parent and depth for each node; no malloc) from the 15 values 5, 12, 20, 27, 33, 41, 47, 50, 58, 63, 70, 74, 81, 88 and 95 inserted in four orders: balanced (middle value first, then the middle of each half), random (a Fisher-Yates shuffle with a 32-bit xorshift generator seeded 20260710), sorted, and alternating (smallest, largest, next smallest, and so on). For each insert record the values compared on the way down, and number the nodes left to right with an in-order walk for drawing. Also build trees of 4 to 256 values (1 to n, in steps of 4) in every order, seeding the shuffle with 20260710 + n. For every tree record the height and the total comparisons to find every value once (depth + 1 each). Publish nb.bst = {values, trees: [{order, inserts, paths, nodes: [{v, x, y, p}], height, compares}], sweep: [{n, order, height, compares}]} with a `__NB_SET__` line, and print the heights and average comparisons for 15 and 256 values.

- **The tree is a set of arrays**: node *i* has `val[i]`, and `left[i]` and `right[i]` hold the numbers of its children, or -1. No `malloc`, so nothing to free and no dangling pointers.
- **`insert` records `path`**, every value compared on the way down. The player replays exactly that walk.
- **`walk`** visits the left subtree, the node, then the right subtree. That visits values smallest first, so the visit number is the node's position across the drawing.

## 3. Watch it grow

> An SVG player for nb.bst, showing the tree for the insert order in nb.bst_order (switching straight away when it changes). Place each node by its in-order number across and its depth down. Play the inserts one at a time: the new value travels as an amber token from the root down its recorded path, each node it is compared with lights up, and a line above narrates the comparisons ("41 < 50, go left · 41 > 27, go right · new right child of 33"); then it settles and its edge appears. Buttons: back to the start, play or pause, next insert; a scrub bar over the inserts; a speed choice. A Find box animates a search for any number the same way and says how many comparisons it took, or where the number would go. A line shows the height and the average comparisons to find a value. Dark theme.

- **The token is the search.** Inserting is just a failed search: walk down comparing, and put the new value where the walk falls off the tree.
- **Each node sits at its in-order number**, so reading the nodes left to right gives the values in sorted order: that's the BST rule made visible.
- **Try *Sorted*.** Every value is bigger than all before it, so each one walks the whole right-hand spine: the tree becomes a 15-long list. *Alternating* fails the same way, zig-zagging.
- **Try the Find box** with 47, then with a number that isn't there, like 60.

## 4. Check the shape

> In JavaScript, check nb.bst: for each of the four 15-value trees, an in-order walk (nodes sorted by their x) must give the values in ascending order, every child must sit on the correct side of its parent, and the height must be the deepest depth plus one. Print a table of order, height, average comparisons (compares divided by the number of values) and whether the checks pass. Then return a Vega-Lite line chart from nb.bst.sweep of average comparisons against the number of values, log scale, one line per order, with log2(n) as a dashed guide, and print the averages at 256 values.

The player shows one tree of 15 values; this cell checks all four and then looks at trees of up to 256 values from the same compute cell.

- **The in-order check** is the BST rule: reading the nodes left to right must give the values smallest first.
- **Average comparisons** is the cost of finding a typical value: the depth of each node plus one, averaged.
- **The log2(n) guide** is roughly the best possible: a perfectly balanced tree halves what's left at every step.

## What the run shows

- **Same values, very different trees.** With 15 values, inserting middle-first gives a tree of height 4: any value is found in at most 4 comparisons, 3.27 on average. A random order gives height 7 and 3.87. Sorted or alternating order gives height 15, a list in disguise: 8.00 comparisons on average, the same as checking a list one by one.
- **All four trees pass the checks.** Read left to right, each gives 5, 12, 20 … 95, and every value sits on the correct side of every ancestor. A badly shaped tree is still a correct tree; it's just slow.
- **At 256 values the gap is huge.** Balanced: height 9, 7.04 comparisons on average. Random: height 15, 8.47. Sorted: height 256, 128.50, eighteen times the balanced cost.
- **Random order is nearly as good as balanced.** On the chart the random line stays close to log2(n), while sorted and alternating climb in a straight line. That's why shuffling input, or a self-balancing tree (AVL, red-black) that rotates nodes to stay short, is used in practice.
- **Data from real input is often sorted.** Timestamps, IDs and alphabetical names all arrive in order: exactly the worst case for a plain BST.

## Try this

Each of these is a prompt. Press **✨** in a cell's header to change its prompt and generate it again, or **⚡ AI Generate New Cell** at the bottom to add a new one.

- **Predict, then pick.** Before choosing *Random*, guess its height: nearer 4 or 15? Then pick it.
- **A self-balancing tree.** Press ✨ on the C cell and add: *"Also build an AVL tree from the sorted order, rotating after each insert to keep it balanced, and publish it as a fifth order called avl."* Then add avl to the dropdown's prompt.
- **Delete a value.** Press ✨ on the C cell and add: *"Then delete 50 from the balanced tree, replacing it with the smallest value of its right subtree, and publish the result as an order called deleted."*
- **Understand the code.** Press the speech bubble (**Explain this cell**) on the C cell and ask why an in-order walk visits the values in sorted order.
